description: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic: every nonzero integer factors uniquely as a product of primes (up to sign and order). Used to define the p-adic valuation v_p and justify that every x ∈ ℚ× writes as ±∏q q^{e_q} uniquely.
Basic commutative ring and field theory: ring homomorphisms, ideals, integral domains, fraction fields, units, quotient rings. Assumed throughout without proof.
Noetherian rings, principal ideal domains (PIDs), unique factorization domains (UFDs), and Krull dimension of a ring. Used in the characterizations of DVRs in Theorem 1.16 and in Corollary 1.23.
Formal power series ring k[[t]] and Laurent series field k((t)): construction, ring/field structure, and the valuation given by the order of vanishing at 0.
Minimal polynomial of an algebraic element α over a field K: the unique monic irreducible polynomial f ∈ K[x] with f(α) = 0. Used in Proposition 1.28 and Example 1.29.

Algebraic closure of a field: every polynomial has a root. Used in the proof of Proposition 1.18 (taking the algebraic closure of the fraction field of A to split f and g) and in Proposition 1.28 (splitting field for the minimal polynomial, yielding conjugates).
Elementary symmetric polynomials and the fact that symmetric polynomials in the roots of f ∈ A[x] lie in A. Used in the proof of Proposition 1.18 to show h = ∏(z − (α_i + β_j)) lies in A[z].

Transitivity of integrality: if C/B/A is a tower with B integral over A and C integral over B, then C is integral over A. The book defers the proof to [1, Thm. 10.27] (Altman–Kleiman) or [2, Cor. 5.4] (Atiyah–MacDonald).
Completions of fields with respect to absolute values, p-adic numbers ℚ_p, and more generally local fields. Mentioned in the Introduction as the broader context and goal; developed in Serre [3].
Function fields over finite fields F_q(t), global fields (number fields and function fields), and their analogy with ℤ. Mentioned in the Introduction as broader context.
Rational root theorem: if r/s ∈ ℚ (in lowest terms) is a root of a monic integer polynomial, then s = ±1. Used explicitly in the proof of Proposition 1.22.
